**Walk (working notes).** Image is about 1280×800, one screen, so I worked from the whole image.

First read: the eye lands on "Crossing the river" at top left, then drops to "Early boats" and reads down the left column. It reads as a short, calm magazine or booklet article about a river ferry's day. Two columns of serif text with three subheads. Quiet and bookish.

Job, assumed: a short reading piece describing a ferry crossing through one day, for a general reader.

The whole piece:
- One-sentence purpose: yes.
- Image and headline make one idea: yes. There is no image, so nothing repeats the headline.
- Every element does a job: yes. There are no rules, boxes or ornament.
- One mood and era: yes. One serif family and one ink colour.
- Copy finished: yes. I found no placeholders or misspellings. "Favourite" is a consistent British spelling.
- Each kind of element looks the same everywhere: yes. The three subheads share one style, and the paragraph indents are the same throughout.
- Colour, shape and direction carry the mood: yes. Black on white and a steady two-column rhythm suit an unhurried piece.
- Each heading names its section: yes. "Early boats", "The market quay" and "Going home" each match their text.

No line was answered no or unsure, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The headings tell the story.** "Early boats", "The market quay" and "Going home" follow the day from morning to night. A reader who only skims the headings still gets the shape of the article. Keep them in time order and keep them concrete.
- **It reads as one whole.** It uses one serif family in a few weights, one ink colour, no ornament, and one indent style for every paragraph. Nothing on the page competes with the text, and that suits a quiet, descriptive piece.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye goes to "Crossing the river" at top left, then down to "Early boats" and into the text. It looks like a short two-column article or feature page about a river ferry, and it feels calm and orderly. Job (assumed): a reading page for general readers.

What matters first:
- One element dominates? **yes.** The title (about 36 px, heavy serif) is clearly the largest and darkest thing on the page.
- Levels distinct at a glance, no near sizes? **yes.** There are three sizes: title about 36 px, headings about 22 px bold, body about 18 px regular. Weight carries the smaller step between heading and body, so each level reads as its own.
- Headings differ in more than size? **yes.** They are bold against regular body text.

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so step 5 has no entries to open.

---

**Section.** What matters first (hierarchy): applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Clear top-down order of three levels.** The title, at about 36 px and heavy, sits well above the section heads, which are about 22 px and bold. The heads sit above the body, which is about 18 px and regular. Each step is large enough, or backed by weight, that a reader can tell title from section from text at a glance. That lets the page be skimmed by its heads ("Early boats", "The market quay", "Going home").
- **Headings set apart by weight as well as size.** The size step from heading to body is fairly small, but the bold weight makes the heads stand out, and they stay in the same serif family. This follows the Refactoring UI idea of "bolder, not bigger". The page stays quiet and consistent but still has an obvious structure.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

Walk (working notes), Arrangement and space, from the whole image at 1280×800. I worked from the whole image because Bash was refused, so I couldn't make crops or open the entries.

1. One grid: yes. Two equal columns at about x 90–595 and 675–1188, with a gutter of about 80 px.
2. No near-misses: no. The right column's first line (top at about y 120) almost lines up with the "Early boats" heading (about y 122) but doesn't sit on it, and it doesn't sit on the left column's first body line (y about 168) either.
3. Baselines across columns: no. Left body lines fall at about 168/193/219, right at about 127/152/178. The right column's heading "Going home" moves it further off (288/313 against 296/321).
4. Space inside groups smaller than between them: yes.
5. Boxes hold one group: yes (there are no boxes).
6. No accidental groups: yes.
7. No overlaps: yes.
8. Margins from the edge: yes.
9. Empty space gathered: no. There is an empty band from about y 545 to 800, the columns end unevenly (540 vs 450), and the area to the right of the title is empty.
10. Balance: no. The weight sits at the top and leans a little left, so the page looks top-heavy.
11. Symmetry chosen for a reason: yes.
12. One proportion for the main divisions: yes (halves).
13. Eye path: yes.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?** and **Do lines of text in neighboring columns sit on the same baselines?**
   - **Where:** the right column starts with body text at about y 120–127. That is almost level with the cap height of "Early boats" (about y 122) but not on it. It is also about 41 px above the left column's first body line (about y 168), which is not a whole number of lines at the roughly 25.5 px leading.
   - **What it does:** every line in the right column sits between two lines on the left, at about 127/152/178 against 168/193/219. After the "Going home" heading the offset changes again (about 288/313 against 296/321), because space around headings isn't a multiple of the leading.
   - **What the reader meets:** reading across the spread, the two columns look slightly out of step, like two separate sheets put side by side rather than one page. The almost-level top edge looks like a mistake rather than a choice.
   - **Fix:** put both columns on one baseline grid. Start the right column on the same baseline as the left column's first body line, or exactly on the heading's line if the flow needs it. Make the space above and below headings add up to whole multiples of the leading so the lines stay level all the way down.
   - **Kind:** convention (aligned baselines across columns is a standard typographic convention). I couldn't open the catalog entries, so I give no specific citation.
   - **Weight:** minor.
2. **Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas, rather than left over in scattered small gaps?** and **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?**
   - **Where:** all the text sits in the top two-thirds of the page. The left column ends at about y 540 and the right at about y 450, which leaves a full-width empty band from about y 545 to 800 (about 30% of the frame) with an uneven top edge. Above it, there's empty space to the right of the title (x 420–1190, y 50–110).
   - **What the reader meets:** the empty space looks left over. The page reads as text that ran out early, and the weight sits at the top and leans a little left, so the frame looks top-heavy and unfinished rather than calm.
   - **Fix:** decide on purpose what the empty space is for. Either balance the columns so they end on the same line and let the bottom margin be one clear, intended area, or fit the page height or text size to the content so the space doesn't pool under it. A deliberately large top margin or a title spanning both columns would also make the empty space look chosen.
   - **Kind:** taste, argued: on a text page, empty space reads as calm only when it sits in one clearly bounded area.
   - **Weight:** minor.

**What's working.**
- Two equal columns with a clear gutter of about 80 px and outer margins of about 90 px on both sides give the page a quiet structure you can see at once. The halves suit continuous reading.
- Headings sit closer to their own text than to the paragraph above. For example, there's about 30 px above "The market quay" and about 15 px below it, so each section reads as one group without rules or boxes.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 9 yes, 4 no (no near-miss alignments; baselines aligned across columns; empty space gathered; visual weight balanced), 0 unsure

**Section.** Text: applies. It is a two-column page of serif running text with a title and three subheads.

**Findings**
1. **Are paragraphs marked by an indent or by space, never both, with the first paragraph after a heading flush left?** The page uses indents only, with no extra space between paragraphs, which is right. But the first paragraph under every heading is still indented: "The first ferry…" (x≈120, y≈167), "The market quay is…" (x≈120, y≈456) and "In the evening…" (x≈705, y≈287). The heading already marks where the paragraph starts, so the indent repeats that signal. It leaves a ~30 px notch at the top-left corner of each block, right under a flush-left heading, and that corner looks ragged. This is Bringhurst's convention: the opening paragraph after a heading is set flush, and only the ones after it are indented. Fix: set the first paragraph after each heading flush left and keep the indent on the ones that follow. Mark: **convention**. Weight: **minor**.
2. **Do paragraphs and columns break cleanly, with no lone short word on a last line and no heading at the foot of a column?** "The market quay" paragraph ends with "flowers." alone on its last line (x≈90, y≈532). It is the last line in the left column, so a lone short word ends the column. The column break itself is also odd. The left column stops at y≈545 with about 250 px of empty white below it, and "The market quay" section then carries on at the top of the right column (y≈127). A reader who reaches "flowers." with all that white space underneath can take it as the end of the section, not a jump to the next column. Fix: rewrap or edit the paragraph so its last line holds more than one word. Then either fill the left column before breaking, or end the section at the column foot so the right column opens with a new heading. Mark: **taste** for the lone word, **defect** for the misleading break. Weight: **minor** (the column-balance part may matter more to the arrangement critic).

**What's working.**
- The body type is set for reading. It is an upright text serif at a comfortable size, around 17 px by eye. The left column's lines look to be about 55–62 characters, inside the 45–75 range Bringhurst gives. The line spacing looks to be about 1.5 times the type size, which suits that line length, so the lines read easily without drifting apart.
- There is one type family with a clear plan: a bold title around 38 px, bold subheads around 22 px, and regular body. Each step is plainly different and used only for its own job. The subheads get more space above than below, so each one sits with the text it introduces.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 28 yes, 2 no (paragraphs marked by an indent or by space, first after a heading flush left; paragraphs and columns break cleanly), 0 unsure
